utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me greet everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, you wanted to speak because you have some correction to make regarding the numbers we got yesterday. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Just to clarify the record for the exhibits admitted yesterday with Witness Donia, I shall read them very slowly. The following exhibits are admitted: P 00002, P 00013, P 00031, P 00089, P 00116, P 00117, P 00132, P 00152, P 00187, P 00192, P 00302, P 00505, P 01043, P 08060, P 09276. The following documents are marked for identification: P 08630, P 08632, P 09537, P 09538, P 09539, P 09540, P 09541, P 09542, P 09543, P 09544, P 09546, P 09547. Finally, the following exhibit is still pending: P 09536. This is the report of expert Donia. This completes the list. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And especially good morning, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I might be skipping from topic to topic because we are trying to condense four days into the next few hours so let me pick off where we left, and we are going to rapidly go subject to subject. I probably won't touch on the banovina since my colleague, Mr. Jonjic, will cover that and other areas, hopefully. Voltaire once noted that conflicts of opinion create problems for historians, especially if those opinions belong to principal figures in a historical account. Would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wise man, that Voltaire. Now, as I understand it from listening to you yesterday and correct me if I'm wrong, in general, historians abstract and select data from descriptions of the events since they were not witnesses to those events themselves, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before we go into the next area, I just want you to make an observation on this particular quote, or it's a paraphrase but it's an observation made by Peter McClelland in Causal Explanations and Model Building in History, Economics and New Economic History. He notes that like journalists, UN observers, social scientists, and diplomats, "historians explain the behaviour of an agent by using statements by the agent, statements by others about the agent, and the actions of the agent as well as their own knowledge, beliefs, and experience, including introspection, making causal explanation in history inherently subjective. Would you agree or disagree with that observation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And with that agreement on that particular observation, off we go. First, let's set some ground rules and decide which areas you are qualified or not qualified. As I understand it, in testifying before this Tribunal on previous occasions, you've indicated you're not a political scientist.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not a political theorist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not a journalist, though you have written some journalistic pieces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not a constitutional lawyer or a constitutional scholar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It would be a fair to say that you're not a ethnographer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And in light of these limitations, may I ask: Did you, in preparing this report or other reports, or in preparing your works, did you ever sit down and analyse the jurisprudence of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The jurisprudence of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By that what I mean is the Statute and all -- so you could be able to at least explain to us how it was set up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have in fact both used and cited the statute. The -- what I've called the founding documents of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well I'm not asking you whether you've cited it. I'm asking you if you've analysed it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've reviewed it and I can read it, see what it says, and concluded what from that is significant to include in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And did you look at any other jurisprudence, rules, regulations, anything that was generated by the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't specifically recall. I looked at several of the statutes that were published in the Narodni List, the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you note that in your -- did you use that for your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was, I take it, provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you -- can you explain to us, for instance, how the HVO was structured?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. This is beyond the scope, completely beyond the scope of the expert. Didn't talk about the structure of the HVO except for a very limited introduction to its establishment, and other witnesses are going to be called on this. It's beyond the scope. Mr. Donia was not asked to opine on this or to review or prepare for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll take that objection to mean that the gentleman is not competent to answer any questions regarding the HVO, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, Your Honour. I said he was not competent. My objection is what it was. My words -- I used my words, not Mr. Karnavas's words. This expert is not here -- did not prepare a report on that topic. It wasn't tendered for such purposes and he can talk -- Mr. Karnavas can ask him questions about everything, talk about the colour of the moon if he wants to, that was not the purpose for which this witness was brought. He has not looked at that. He was not asked to look at this. Mr. Tomanovic and other people will be addressing these matters for which they have specifically been named on our witness list and the Chamber is aware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note that in the written expert report, within the table of contents, there is a -- the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, page 39. Let me take page 39. And what do I find there? The HVO was created on the 8th of April. The executive, military, and political powers are concentrated in the hands of this sole institution which has -- is responsible before the HZ HB. So please continue, Mr. Karnavas, if you want to put questions to this witness about pages 39 and 40. You are free to do so because you can cross-examine on the written statement by the witness, although Mr. Scott pointed out quite rightly that we will have an expert speaking about the HVO, but a historian usually has a wide scope of competence, even though he may not be a demographer, specialist in political sciences, as a historian he has to deal with specific sectors. He spoke about the HVO in his written report. It is therefore quite normal that a question should be put about the HVO. If he doesn't know, he'll say, "I don't know." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to go into too many details about the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But generally, well, were you asked in Blaskic, back then, this was 1997, who created it and you indicated you did not know. This was on page 848 to 849 of the transcript. Does that -- do you stand by that answer today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One of the benefits of being a historian is that there is a constant process of discovery that goes on and so I've noted somethings that I didn't know about in 1997 which I really -- may or may not have been available at that time but I was not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the conclusion that I've drawn which Mr. President has just read represents the essence of my understanding of the formation of the HVO and its fundamental structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the report in front of me so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was structured?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who composed it? Who were members of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's see, 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And other than that, you can't help us out on the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the Presidency, the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear four different questions there. Which one would you like me to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Other than naming Mate Boban and telling us that he is the president of the Presidency, other than that, you're not able to provide us any more details about the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you. Mr. Scott. I didn't hear you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object again to the form of the question. What the examiner put questions to the witness, specific questions to the witness about, can you tell us anything else or I take it you can't tell us anything else. Let him ask specific questions of the witness not just open-ended -- so I assume you can't tell us anything else. Mr. Donia may be able to say other things but the examiner lass to put proper questions to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President I don't mean to be giving a lecture but yesterday when the Prosecutor should have been asking direct questions he was asking cross-examination questions and yet today he's telling me how to do cross by way of asking direct questions. I merely stated or asked a question, if the gentleman doesn't -- can't answer the question he can say so. I haven't prevented him from not expanding, go ahead and give explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine. We are not going to waste any more of our precious time. You asked the witness whether he was in a position to provide you with other names of members of the Presidency. He answered that he could not. So please move on to another question. He mentioned Mate Boban but apart from him he wasn't aware of any other names, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to the Presidency and the HVO, do you know what that relationship was, if any?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had reference to the document creating it, I could tell you exactly what it is. And my -- I'm not really prepared to speculate based on my recollection of that document. It's something that I looked at in the course of the preparation of the report. I spelled it out in the report. It is there in black and white, and I'm sure if I had reference to the report, I might be able to say something more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now you say the document. Are you referring to the document of the establishment of the HZ HB and the HVO or are you saying your report? Which of the two or both?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two documents that would be relevant to this are the document creating the HZ HB and the document creating the HVO, and the additional documents which expand the functions and jurisdiction of those two bodies which I have addressed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't mean to press you on this one but if we had those documents, could we not read them for ourselves? Do we need a historian to tell us what those documents say? Do we need an expert to come here and testify as to those legal documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would argue that, yes, you do. I think that putting them in a context is what is important in terms of my function or role here. There is, I think, a level of analysis, let's say a legal analysis, which I don't pretend to address and which is indeed something that is -- that I willingly leave to others but I think that the developmental picture that's presented in these documents is worthy of historical note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again I don't mean to press you nor do I mean to be -- to put you in a bad light but you testified in Blaskic in 1997, then you were in Kordic, I don't remember the date, I think it was 1999 or 2000, then I take it before coming here you met with the Prosecution to proof for this presentation, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact you probably spent the whole day with them before you came here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, just a few hours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe three, four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Three, four hours. And you read your report before you came here to meet with the gentleman, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it in writing the report, you probably sent them a draft and he might have asked you to add some things or correct some things?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So he had an opportunity to review the report and ask you to supplement it. So, again, I don't mean to be pressing you but how is it after all these years, being an expert, you say to us today that you need to look at these documents in order to put them into a historical context when in fact you would have had to have looked at them, analysed them, absorbed them, synthesised them, in order to come up with the conclusions which you have in your report? How is that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've again distorted my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I used those documents to create a brief narrative in the section on the HZ HB, and on the HVO. I put them into a historical context. I think I've at least started to put them into a historical context here and that context is a developmental one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins with the creation of the HZ HB in November 1991, proceeds to an expansion of its powers in a series of constitutional changes, I believe in April and June of 1992, the creation of the HVO as a -- as I said fused, synthetic organisation or body in -- on the 8th of April 1992, and proceeds from there to further strengthen its competencies on the basis of its self-proclaimed constitutional changes, and its jurisdiction over its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now I just want to hit a couple of high points or quick points and then we'll move on. Yesterday you noted to us when you were asked about the various parties, one in particular the SDA, that was the Muslim national -- I prefer to use that term as opposed to nationalist and we will have a discussion on that but that was the Muslim national party, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you came to that point, you had indicated that there was some disagreement as to what sort of name to choose and that's why they went with SDA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for the record that can be found on page 65, lines 9 through 14. You say -- you know, I just want to be precise, "the meetings resulted in the formulation of a party platform and the decision to give the party a non-national name. That is, the term Bosnian Muslim or Bosniak does not appear in the name party of the democratic action party because leaders couldn't agree on exactly how to formulate the party's desired constituency in terms of nomenclature that they would all accept." You stand by that answer that you gave yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's inappropriate for the cross-examining attorney to have a copy of a document that I wrote when I don't have it to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was your statement yesterday. This was your statement yesterday. Just calm down. Please get this gentleman his notes. You know, I didn't tell you not to come in with your notes, your report. You had it there yesterday. If the Prosecutor would like to help the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, It was provided through the Registry yesterday and perhaps -- I assume what happened is that someone collected it from the witness stand last night. I'm sure we can obviously get another copy but if it's not -- there is not one immediately available from the Registry we will collect another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Mr. Donia, you need your report in order to refresh your memory. Because there are points that need to be looked into, right? And you need to examine the report to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding. Mr. Karnavas is not quoting your report. He is quoting the transcript of what you deposited, what you said here and that you can probably find on the screen and maybe they will then show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be most help so that I know that he's not taking it out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I just read it to you sir, but again it's on page 65. I can even provide the -- we are going to talk about taking things out of context, but it can be found on page 65, lines 9 through 14. I can read the full question and answer if you would prefer that, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you like me to read the full question and the answer, sir? Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please read out page 65, lines 9 to 14, because the witness does not have yesterday's transcript before him. So please remind him of his statement. If you want to do so you have to read it out. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President I'll start with line 1. [French translation coming over English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Nationalist party of the Bosnian Muslims. Its origins may be found in some meetings that took place between Alija Izetbegovic, who, like Tudjman, was a dissident, who had been imprisoned in socialist Yugoslavia and in fact released only months before the party was formed, and other Bosnian Muslim leaders, including Adil Zulfikarpasic who was living at the time in Switzerland. The meetings resulted in the formulation of a party platform and the decision to give the party a non-national name. That is, the term Bosnian Muslim or Bosniak does not appear in the name Party of Democratic Action partly because the leaders couldn't agree on exactly how to formulate the party's desired constituency in terms of nomenclature that they would all accept. Do you recall giving that answer yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Congratulations on your pronunciation of Zulfikarpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's taken sometime, trust me. Now I looked at your -- I read your statement. We have been referring to it as an expert report. And on page 21, under the section Party of Democratic Action, SDA, you state here, and I'll start with the first paragraph, "Bosnian Muslim organisers taking the first step toward create ago political party convened an initiating committee on March 27, 1990, defining their party ambiguously as political alliance of citizens of Yugoslavia who belong to the Muslim culture, historical circle, they chose a name the Party of Democratic Action, SDA," I won't even bother to read the B/C/S -- Bosniak or Bosnian language "so as to circumvent the legal ban on parties based on a single religion or nation." So the name, according to your report, was chosen to circumvent, I underscore that, to circumvent the legal ban, not because they could not agree on a particular name. Would you not agree with me that those are two different answers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you'll refer to my answer in testimony yesterday, I used the word "partly."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the other part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see, that's the -- right. The -- in my verbal testimony yesterday, I used the word "partly" to indicate that that was one of the reasons that they -- they could not agree on a name and the reason they could not agree on the name was that the best known proponent of the Bosniak name for the group was in fact Mr. Zulfikarpasic who was at that time really one of the two key leaders of the party. The ultimate decision to make a -- to choose the name certainly involved this effort to circumvent the ban on parties based on historical or -- I'm sorry, national or religious grounds, and it isn't totally clear to me in going through the documentation which was the more important or which was the first consideration that they entered into but clearly both considerations played a role in awarding the name to the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Of course, we have to take into consideration that at the time, as you noted yesterday, there was a law in place, was it not, banning such parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That law was passed, as I said, in February of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time, the other parties, the HDZ and the SDS, had not been formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were furiously organising at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Organising but had not been formed. You have different dates. The first one is to form themselves and organise themselves into a party was the SDA, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- again you're using the founding assemblies as the critical event in the formation. I looked at the long string of conferences, meetings, formations of provisional committees as a part of the organising process and therefore in all three cases, far predating the passage of that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Another point, maybe very quickly we can get at, yesterday you had indicated that there was a rift within the HDZ and there were two factions and as a result, two particular individuals were canned, were sacked, one of them being Mr. Lasic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't testify yesterday that Mr. Lasic was sacked. We have the statement from Mr. Karadzic in the Bosnian Serb assembly that he was removed from the delegation to the Cutileiro talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to have to find your statement from yesterday to make sure I get it right. Franjo Boras do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But do you know of him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who exactly is he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the -- one of two Croatian members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina elected in November of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe it was Mr. -- I'm told, I don't have it present with me but I'm told that Mr. Boras in his book indicates that Mr. Lasic was indeed at Cutileiro, and this would have been back in March 1992. Could you possibly be wrong on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony was that Karadzic said that Lasic had been removed from the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what Karadzic. But you know, the OTP is running around trying to find him. We don't know where he is to question him. Other than Karadzic, what he said, do you have any other information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- yes. I -- Mr. Lasic was on a list of people who attended at least one of the sessions of the negotiating process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in spite of that rift, and in spite of having a disagreement, and we are going to get to that December 27, 1991, presidential transcript, in spite of that, he participated a few months thereafter in one of these talks, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the map that was generated from Cutileiro -- I'm getting ahead of myself again but if we looked at that map, that was pretty favourable to the Muslims, was it not, as far as land?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which map -- which of the four maps are we talking about, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There are four maps in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll get to this point later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, sticking with Mr. Lasic, and I have it -- I'm looking at a document here, agreement of 3 March 1993 between Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Mate Boban, and Mile Akmadzic. You know all these gentlemen, you know their names?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it indicates that Mr. Lasic was being proposed, okay, that they have submitted the following six names to serve in the interim Presidency, Fikret Abdic, Mile Akmadzic, Franjo Boris, Ejup Ganic, Alija Izetbegovic, and Miro Lasic. This would have been in 3 March 1993. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I'm not looking at the document. I can't -- can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether Mr. Lasic was proposed to be on the interim Presidency in 3 March 1993, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour if the examiner is going to put questions to the witness about a document, I ask that the document be shown to the witness. That's a fundamental fairness, that the document be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no objections to showing the document. I'm asking from his memory whether he knows that, yes or no, back in 1993, 3 March. Do you know whether he was proposed, yes or no? I'm trying to save some time as opposed to showing documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was proposed to be on the interim Presidency, yes, no, maybe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you just told me and I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't know then. From your independent knowledge and experience and all this research you've been doing, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I walked in here this morning, I did not have that specific date and document in my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Assuming that he was proposed, okay, would that cut against, again, your argument or your assertion yesterday that somehow because he voiced a separate opinion or a different opinion than others on 27 December 1991, that he was still within the fold, the family, of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question without seeing that document and knowing perhaps even more about the background to that. I think it's worth remembering that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina included Stjepan Kljuic for almost all of that time. I believe he resigned in -- I don't remember the date but it was somewhere in either late 1992 or early 1993, under pressure from the HDZ and then resumed that position later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and this is the only gentleman that you -- that you've interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. And again you've misrepresented what I said in earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I can name some names. Of all the Presidencies, of all the individuals that served on the Presidencies, did you interview Boris, let's just say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Who of the presidents of the Presidency or members of the Presidency did you interview?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from that period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, speaking of Mr. Kljujic and speaking of the minutes -- speaking of the presidential transcript, I take it you've read that, this is the one of the 27th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's a fairly lengthy one, is it not, it's about 70 pages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you read it more than once?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read portions of it probably a dozen times. Other parts perhaps twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I had anticipated spending about an hour to two hours with you on that but we don't have that time so perhaps with few questions we might get through. Fair to say this was a meeting where a lot of individuals participated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall about how many?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I at one point counted about 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it seems that everyone or many of them are voicing a particular opinion or have statements to make?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Be fair to say that you have to read the entire document, the entire document, as opposed to taking out one sentence or part of a sentence or a phrase in order to get the full flavour and context of what exactly was happening at that particular meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We might also say that you might even have to look at other events, what was happening in Croatia, what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was happening in Serbia, what was happening in the international community, to also try to get a flavour and an understanding, the contextual background, of some of the topics that were being discussed during that meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that if we go through that document, and I'm prepared to do so but I don't think we are going to be sitting past 1.45, though I'm perfectly willing to do so, just in case Mr. President has changed his mind, it would be fair to say that many individuals had different opinions, different proposals, with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina on the issue of the Croatian question, if I can put it so pedestrian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And Tudjman, the late President Tudjman, as you well know, was a historian, was he not, in his previous -- before he came a president, he was a historian. We will talk a little bit about his life?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. He has a pretty good grasp of the past history of the Croatian peoples and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And, of course, there are times when he's asking questions during this presidential transcript?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean he's chairing the meeting, more or less, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is chairing most of it, at least, and is clearly a dominant figure in the room when he's in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the meeting, you can almost get a sense that there was a little tension in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call it a great deal of tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, all right. Certain personalities had different views and they were clashing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a distinct clash of views. It was very personalised by the various parties directed mainly against, but not exclusively against, Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that Tudjman throughout this meeting that he's chairing, at times would ask a question but in the question may you may walk away with an impression of what he's thinking about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But fair to say that there is one consistent thread throughout this discussion with respect to the late President Franjo Tudjman and that is that he's urging those the next to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to speak with the two other main interlocutors, and that is Karadzic and Izetbegovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No? Okay. That's -- you didn't see that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll break it up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that there was one consistent thread throughout this discussion and the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Does he not urge the parties to go back and talk to Alija Izetbegovic and Karadzic and try to find some negotiated settlement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, he says it more than once?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to Kljujic, since you mentioned him, at that point in time he was the head of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And is this -- is this meeting before or after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum on independence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about two months before the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. There is a -- now, Mr. Kljujic has his points of views as well. Do you recall him saying, on page 2, I'm just going to read it, you could just tell me if you agree or disagree with having read it, since you've read it and analysed it, he says "We stated our position clearly a year ago that we were for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, as long as there was a shred of a chance that it may come to pass." I have an extra copy if you would like to see it, to follow along. If I could have the assistance -- And I believe this is P 00089. We are just going to cover a couple of these things. I don't -- you would find it where it starts with the paragraph, "For us and for the HDZ, there were no dilemmas in this respect because this was our party's platform as well and we stated our position clearly a year ago, that we were for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as there was a shred of a chance that it may come to pass." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the next page, page 3, where it begins, the paragraph says, "Finally," I don't want to read it but there is a discussion there with respect to currency, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The dinar. That would have been the dinar that was coming in from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a problem that they were facing in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a problem facing essentially all of the former Yugoslavia at the time, and that was the weakness and effectively devaluation of the dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But the currency, the Serbian dinar being used in Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of the issues, and I believe, and maybe you can help me out here, that the Croats at that time saw that perhaps with the use of the Serbian dinar, Bosnia-Herzegovina could be going closer and closer to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one, let's say, bell weather indicator that they were watching to see let's say the direction in which particularly the Bosnian Muslim leadership might move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, had Croatia been attacked by the JNA by there point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So that might be one reason why they might have some suspicions and fears, or at least what was happening from Belgrade, what Belgrade was doing, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had been at war for essentially most of the year, certainly for six months, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by this point, I take it, that incident in Ravno would have happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident in Ravno was in, I think, October 4th or 5th of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, and that was a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe there was another incident prior to that, I believe it was in May 1991, a smaller incident but nonetheless it involved Croatians, that's in Uniste [phoen]? If you don't recall, that's fine, or if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But fair to say, and I'm sure you might know this, that the JNA was using Bosnian territory from which to launch attacks against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- you could characterise it as a -- the major JNA staging area for the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, Izetbegovic did nothing to prevent that, did he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was action by the Presidency, the critical issue for the JNA at that point was manpower, massive desertions, and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina urged its -- the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to disregard the mobilisation of reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, is it not a fact that the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, who was proclaiming to be the president for all peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did nothing to prevent the JNA from using Bosnian territory to attack Croatia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall him saying, this is not our problem? This is not our war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the war he meant, the war that was going on in Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The same war where the belligerent army was using his territory in order to attack another country, Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the Croats that were living just over the border in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you could consider them as, in a sense, co-nationals, since they shared the same national identity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: History, culture, literature, language, religion, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at least one might walk away thinking, you know what? Maybe this president is not looking after our interests. Maybe he's not protecting us, especially when a Croatian village is demolished, people are killed, they are Croatian by origin and the response of the president is, not our war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the response of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Ravno incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I said the president. I didn't say the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the president of the Presidency was Alija Izetbegovic, and he and other members of the Presidency dispatched a delegation to Ravno to investigate what had happened and come back, make recommendations. So again I insist it is not the case that the Presidency, nor the president of the Presidency, did nothing. I'm not happy that they didn't do more, myself, but your flat statement that they did nothing is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By this point, was the SDA arming itself, their military wing, the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By this time, you know, Ravno time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was an army, so to speak, by Muslims for Muslims, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd call it a paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Paramilitary. All right. You also had the TO, the Territorial Defences, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And depending on where they were located because they were usually by design they were -- they came under the municipalities, you know, there may be a mixture depending on the municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Do you know how the Territorial Defences were structured?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And was there Territorial Defence for the entire country at Sarajevo that was their headquarters or was it -- we have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could we have some timeframes for these things? These things were changing day to day, week to week. During this time period, there was the JNA TO Territorial Defence, later there was the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence. So could we have timeframes, please, for these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The time frame for my learned friend, had he been listening, is the Ravno time. That was the previous questions were for, the Ravno time. We've already established that Ravno happened September or so in 1991. Where is the dilemma that Mr. Scott is having other than trying to eat up my time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with that period of time, 1991, in September, could you tell us how the Territorial Defences were structured?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was a republican-level organisation. It existed in all republics of the former Yugoslavia, and reported jointly to the JNA command, and to the Ministry of Defence of the individual republics. In effect, many Territorial Defence units at this time were under the control of municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many municipalities, that meant essentially no change from the time that they had been operating as a kind of a standby or reserve force which was a very wide -- there was widespread participation in it. In some other instances the Territorial Defence units were under the control of municipal authorities of a particular national party. In some cases, the HDZ, in some cases, the SDS, and in relatively few cases, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The SDA also had -- well there was these Green Berets, they were also Muslim fighters, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were really at this time in the beginning stages of being formed. Neither one of them really took off until the war in Croatia started to cause many Muslim participants in the JNA to desert, come back to Bosnia, and volunteer for these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Might one say that they volunteer for these forces because they saw the winds, you know, changing, was switching direction, that perhaps they would be next, in other words Bosnia-Herzegovina might be next on the attack list by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it would make sense, for instance, for these communities to organise themselves, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which communities are you speaking of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, communities within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What communities are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's just say the municipalities. Would it be fair to say that the municipalities should become more actively engaged in mobilising themselves, in preparation for war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that was a republican function, and there were some municipalities who did undertake that, but by and large under leadership of their political leaders based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the establishment of the Patriotic League, that was not a republican function, was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go back to Mr. Kljujic, at some point, I'm just going to because we are eating up quite a bit of time here, on page 7, it's still Mr. Kljujic, if you look at page 6, and then you go to page 7, he says here, middle of the page, "Gentlemen I think everything is clear to someone who adopts language like that." He's referring to Karadzic from the previous sentence, and he says, "I think it would be acceptable to have a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina divided into cantons which would guarantee human rights to all, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not following you where you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 7?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 7, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wants to make sure that we're still with Kljujic. "I think that it would be acceptable to have a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina divided into cantons which would guarantee human rights to all but to partition Bosnia according to the Serbian recipe would put us in a minority position as we constitute over 50 per cent of the population in 14 municipalities while in five municipalities we have a plurality." So at least from this statement it appears, does it not, that Mr. Kljujic is suggesting or he's -- he's accepting the possibility of cantons in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he did, and virtually everyone in the top political leadership, even social democrats, accepted the possibility that cantons would evolve from the negotiating process, and the SDA leaders, for example, who were in principle opposed to that division, nevertheless came up with maps for the creation of cantons. They didn't like the name of the game that they were playing but, forced to play it, they were determined to play it well. And this is what I take to be Kljujic's feelings about the matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- and what is ultimately proposed or being discussed at Cutileiro looks like cantons, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks like a division into ethnic, I would say, enclaves, and the problematic part of this for all parties was the lack of continuity within the Cutileiro plan. It chopped these territories up into two, three, four units per group, making communication and compactness of territory, to use the words of the Graz agreement, impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, the Croats were willing to accept their lot and sign off on it, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear that they signed off on -- I'm quite sure that they did not sign the Cutileiro agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But is there not -- there is a principle agreement that all three parties initially come to terms with, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I stand corrected. The Croats agreed, correct, and so does Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Help me out here, then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the statements made by the leaders of the three parties as they emerge from the talks, if you look at the post-talk commentary on the talks at the time of the London Conference in August of 1992, everyone seems to agree that there was never anything specifically agreed to. They only accepted verbally the map as a basis for further talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I misstated that. And after accepting the map for further talks, did anyone change their mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question. They all refused to, let's say, proceed on that basis, and engaged in a game of mutual blame throwing right up until the time of the independence recognition, April 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Cutileiro plan itself, it's sort of was based on three constituent units, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Based on national principles and taking into account the economic, geographical and other criteria, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that Bosnia-Herzegovina would continue to have its existing borders, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're reading something. I'm not too sure what you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question. I mean, you're the expert, you're telling me that you analysed these documents. Isn't that what the Cutileiro plan provided for, not the carving up of Bosnia. It would have its existing borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in -- in principle, what the Cutileiro plan proposed, yes. I don't want to be held to the specific wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I think at no time did it propose that it break up into three different countries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean formally? Did -- informally they were to break up into three different countries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the term formally in the same sense that President Tudjman did in the December 27th meaning nominally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But again, did we not -- I thought we had an agreement that you had to look at all of the -- his entire, that entire meeting that 70 pages, in order to come to some kind of a conclusion as to what his position is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his position is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I am going to read from the document. And it's -- it would be 1 D 00398. If we could go to the page 24 of the -- I guess it would be at the bottom of the page, 1D 190034. Perhaps it would be easier to put it on the ELMO since I just want to make some quick points. Thank you. All right. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And under item 1 it says, three constituent units, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And those three constituent units, by the way, those were already guaranteed in the BiH constitution, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I misspoke. The nations -- there were three constituent nations in the BiH constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three constituent nations in the BiH constitution without any assignment of any territorial division among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But there were three nations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three constituent nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And sorry, here we have three constituent units. Now you go to number 2, Bosnia-Herzegovina would continue to have its existing borders, nothing about carving up, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina nor the governments of the constituent units, that would be the Croat, the Serb and the Muslim, will encourage or support claims to any part of its territories by neighbouring states, all right? That's under number 2?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then number 3, sovereignty resides in the citizens of the Muslim, Serbs and Croat nations, and other nations and nationalities who realise it through their civic participation in the constituent units and the central organs of the republic, all right? And now they seem to be making a distinction between nations and nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we are talking about nations, you know, this -- we said that the constitution guaranteed three nations, it's a little bit different than a nationality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Yugoslav legal theory a nation was one which had a constituent status in a republic. A nationality was typically a people whose corpus was principally outside Yugoslavia but had a representation of population within it, such as, for example, Hungarians, Albanians in Kosovo, Italians in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for the Croats, at least in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was rather important because by demographics, they only composed about 17.5 of the population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to parse the statement, I think the notion of each -- for each group, the status of constituent nation was critically important. The disagreement came on whether that sovereignty would be realised through the constituent units --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- In whole or in part, or whether it was in fact a function of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Even at the -- at the national level, Yugoslavia, that was kind of an issue that was coming up, that had come up, at least, with free elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The issue of nations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a critical [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday you touched upon it a little bit, about unitary government, that issue. I believe Mr. Scott asked you a question or two about that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was just the preface. Do you recall, have you ever heard the term unitary government?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in this particular context, did it not mean one person, one vote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different concept completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. At that time, was it not -- isn't it a fact that for the Croats, they opposed the principle of one person, one vote, on a general basis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Some. Are you saying 5 per cent, 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was not one of the main issues because of their -- they were only 17.5 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of their percentage of the population was that -- and continues to be a critical -- of critical concern to Croatian leaders, nationalist and non-nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that an issue for the Croats and the Slovenes during the Yugoslav days as Milosevic was grabbing and amassing power?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit different. The situation of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia, and their relationship to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a constitutional one at the republican federal level, couldn't quite touch on these issues of sovereignty within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Needless to say, the Croatians were worried about their vital, national interests, Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because of their percentage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was concerned about their vital, national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about everyone. I asked you about the Croatians. If you can answer me, answer my question. We will talk about the others afterwards.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian in Bosnia-Herzegovina were definitely concerned about their status, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you look at those numbers, they are pretty low?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the lowest of the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that when the Croats voted for the referendum -- during the referendum, for independence, that was more of a vote against being part of Bosnia-Herzegovina being part of Yugoslavia or what was left of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair characterisation of the leadership of the HDZ's understanding at that time. I think that aptly captures their motivation. You know, what the individual voter of Croatian nationality was thinking is hard to know. I think there were probably as much as anything a desire to follow the party leadership in whatever call they made, and a general sense of in many cases a feeling that Bosnia-Herzegovina ought to be an independent republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But the Serbs objected to that, right, they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia and that's why they went off on their own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- okay. Now, to your knowledge, maybe you can help us out here, did Alija Izetbegovic ever state a position, and, if so, where, as to how he envisaged protecting the vital national interests of the Croatian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina, how he would exactly do that, other than promoting the one person, one vote, which would always give them the majority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not in a position to give you a specific quotation, but there are hundreds, probably thousands of times in which Izetbegovic stood by the principle of the equal rights for every constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore, of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, equal rights but he also maintained a consistent policy of one person, one vote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was sort of an issue, a burning issue in Iraq, with the Shiite, they wanted that one person, one vote, because they had 60 per cent of the population with the Shiite being only 20 per cent and the Kurds another 20 per cent, they would always be outvoted. So in that context one might say one person, one vote would not necessarily promote at least to the Croatian satisfaction their vital national interest. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boy, I've -- I lost you there, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Can't answer that question? Too complex?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can repeat it, I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Are you following the events in Iraq where they are trying to draft a constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they are not trying to draft a constitution. They drafted a constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's right. And the first proposal that was on the table was one person, one vote, which the Shiite were promoting. Bush didn't count on it, on promoting democracy, but they were insisting one person, one vote, 60 per cent, they win every time, and that was one of the main stumbling blocks, was it not, for the Kurds and the Sunni?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me go to the one part of your question which perhaps isn't -- the answer hasn't been made completely clear. In the voting for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a system which was backed by the SDA and Izetbegovic which was not strictly one man one vote. It assured the Croats equal participation with Serbs and Muslims in terms of the two representatives on the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. With the third one going to the other, being a Muslim who claimed to be a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The voting for the category of other was available to any candidate who declared himself something other than those three groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that's at the party leadership. Going down, in other positions, did they have a formula to ensure at the lower ranks within the bureaucracy, that that would -- that formula would be adhered to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a complex question, that was very much respected at the -- you know, in the, say, early to mid-eras of socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We are talking now. We are talking now. I don't want to talk about socialism. We are into democracy now. So let's not backtrack. I'm talking about at this point, because you mentioned it. What about other organs in the assembly in the municipalities, did they have a formula throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina so that they would protect the vital national interests of the Croatian people who were 17.5 of the population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, there was a formula in effect in the Presidency, that is not a party organ, that is a state organ of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The interparty agreement which was reached on the eve of the voting in November of 1990, assured participation to all groups according to a formula, as I indicated yesterday, that applied in every municipality and was in fact implemented in the first six months of 1991 in most municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it's not a simple matter of one person, one vote, versus a single formula. There were multiple formulas and changes going on in the bureaucracy that resulted in, in some cases more Croats coming into certain bodies, in other cases fewer. The point I was trying to make is that as, particularly professional organisations under socialism, developed criteria for hiring which were not national. When the democratic elections took place in November of 1990, in many cases the national parties came along and attempted to establish an ethnic balance according to formulas agreed upon which overrode the professional principles of selection of these various organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that your full answer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like more?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, is it not a fact that the term unitary government and one person, one vote, was a burning issue, particularly for the Croats, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say for many Croats, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in part, it was because of the reasons that I stated, this they were concerned about their vital national interests, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One might even say that there was a vital national interests and how they were going to be protected, could be seen in the manner in which the president handled the Ravno incident, and him allowing Bosnia-Herzegovina territory to be used as a staging ground for a belligerent army to attack a nation which was occupied by co-nationals that shared the same culture, the same history, the same language, so when you put all of it together, you can understand how the Croats might have been concerned in that particular time, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your testimony, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Now, we have about five minutes before the break. Perhaps we could just touch upon one quick issue, switch to a different topic. Yesterday you talked about the Croatian constitution and you mentioned that the banovina was mentioned in the preamble of the constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I noticed you stopped there. You stopped at the banovina. You didn't go on. Now, perhaps we could look at that document and in fairness to you but also in fairness to President Tudjman and all the other drafters, in order to put it in context I think it would be good to look at it. This would be is 1D 00400. I'm sorry, it's actually already in as P 8532. Perhaps it might be easier as well to have it on the ELMO. I don't know, whichever is most convenient. If it's going to take some time I do have a copy. If we could just look at that, just -- and you have to -- can we zoom down so we could see the whole -- a little bit more, a little bit more, a little bit more. Of course, you can't read it now but if you look at that, that first part, it talks -- it's titled, "historical foundations," if I can read it correctly. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that, it sort of covers an entire period of the Croatian people's history, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say the Croatian people and state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And state. Okay. And so naturally there was one period within their history where the banovina came into, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But they don't stop there. It continues, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if we look at this in context, in context, it's not highlighting the banovina, it's merely referencing, referencing, the banovina, as part of the Croatian history of the peoples and of the territories of the Croatian peoples, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's highlighting about what's the seven or eight particular -- I counted them once, I think it's more than that, I think it's nine or ten, significant events in the history of the Croatian state and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of which the creation of the banovina is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so if you were going to read the constitution for the very first time, if you were a Croat in a period where for the first time at least in modern history they have what they believe is a free and democratic society, reading that part of the Croatian constitution, be they Croat or somebody else, at least would put them into the picture of what it means to be a Croat and what is the basic Croatian foundational history, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so even if we just take the banovina out and highlight it, are we not taking it out of context?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you just take out, no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we are because the broader context of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You answered the question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of course, that the Croatian state was not simply made up of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made up of 600 and some thousand Serbs. It was made up of other nationalities. And so the broader context of this is that when we talking about the history of the Croatian state --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's one thing. But when we go into the history of the Croatian people and make the history of the these highlighted items, the history of the Croatian people, that excludes a certain population, and the banovina was particularly egregious in this respect.
