So in my view that's what makes this an important I would say key element of this. I would say -- I would agree that the ideal way to present this is in fact to give you the entire constitution and note that this is one of the provisions for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I put to you, sir, that that answer is somewhat of a confabulation, and that in fact you took it out of context and you drew it to our attention not because they failed to mention a particular peoples but rather you are pushing the Prosecution's agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. It's not even a question, it's purely a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm putting my case to the witness, he can answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I still object to it. I don't care if he's putting his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, objection, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because this is purely -- all this is, is Mr. Karnavas arguing his case and not only arguing his case but taking it completely out of context. There was no effort to put an isolated sentence in front of the Chamber. The claim has the entire constitution. That was given to you and the only testimony that's been about that is that one part of it makes reference that the banovina is mentioned in the Croatian constitution, a point that appears to be not in dispute. It's mentioned in the Croatian constitution and that's the only point and the rest of it is argument. The rest of it is purely Mr. Karnavas making argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Just before we have our break, Mr. Karnavas, you were asking a question of the witness about the fact that the banovina was omitted or was taken out of the constitution, but as was pointed out by Mr. Scott, as I note myself, in the historical foundation, mention is made of the banovina in 1939. So I fail to quite follow you in your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the argument made by the Prosecutor in response, their objection, actually drove the point home and I accept what they just indicated the objection to be. If it was just mentioning the banovina, that's fine. And I think now we have some clarification, we can no longer place any more emphasis on that factor since it's merely mentioned. Thank you. In regards to this context of how it was raised, with pointing it out in the constitution. The banovina may play another role in a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now 10.35. Let's have a 20-minute break and we shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We left off on the banovina. As I indicated Mr. Jonjic will cover that but since we were speaking about banovinas, I thought we would touch a little bit on Franjo Tudjman. Yesterday you said that he was quite open, quite frank, and has written extensively on his particular views, the views he held, be they political or historical. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you, being a historian, have read everything that Franjo Tudjman has written?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read his books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I've read every article or speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But his primary works, you've read?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially the ones going back when he was a director of the -- just know it by the acronym, the IHRPH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Institute for Contemporary History and -- I think it's Institute for Contemporary History is the name of the institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was a director of that after he had left the JNA, as I understand it. He had been a general in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He grew up or was brought up through the Partizan movement, prominent member of the Communist Party, purged to some extent, and he had a rather colourful and distinguished career, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And some may even liken him, at least when he began to voice his opinion, back in the -- that period called or known as the Croatian spring and being a reformer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some certainly viewed him as a reformer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We are talking about a communist, not a socialist. I know they use the word socialist but, let's face it, it was a communist system, it may be communist light to some when you compare it to maybe East Germany but nonetheless it was communist, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you indicated, he went to prison a couple of times in his lifetime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you shared with us some -- I believe it was from Owen's book, his opinion or at least a little vignette of Mr. -- the late President Tudjman's position, at least with respect to how Owen recalled it. Have you by any chance read what the former ambassador, American ambassador, I believe his name is Herbert Okun, said about his dealings with Mr. Tudjman? Have you come across that at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we can put it on the ELMO or if we have it in the new system, on the ELMO? I apologise for going low-tech but I prefer it this way in some ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very high-tech but it is very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could just give it a quick glance, I assume that you're a quick reader, being an intellectual. And I have the Croatian version, if you want. This is a draft translation. Okay. Have you had a chance to look at it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me another minute to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. This is part we are looking at, by the way, this is 1D 00416, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the ELMO if we could flip the page so we could see the B/C/S version of it for our B/C/S speakers and also if you could just look at that, do you know this gentleman or know of him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. American ambassador, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign service officer of ambassador rank, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And his opinion of Tudjman is rather that he is straightforward, serious politician, kept his word, honest, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Curt in style, you know, curt style of behaviour, which many, especially journalists of the west misinterpreted. Was that your opinion of Tudjman as well? I know you haven't met him but --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many journalists in the west? Yes, I think that's a good observation. Journalists did in fact, I think, misinterpreted most of these leaders in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And one would expect the ambassador who is having dealings, someone of ambassador rank, if he's having dealings as it would appear that Mr. Okun suggests that they might have a better opportunity to see them and not just formal but also informal settings from which they could draw some opinions and conclusions, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding was that Okun was Vance's notetaker and companion as he was negotiating what became the Vance Plan in January of 1992. So he would have had some occasions and perhaps missed others, if those meetings were one on one between Vance and Tudjman but I would agree with your proposition, he had ample opportunity to observe Tudjman and relate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we at least we get a pretty good picture, at least from this particular gentleman, of his impressions of the late President Tudjman and might you conclude from reading this that they are rather positive and not negative?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we can move on. And thank you very much, Madam Usher. Yesterday, I think the -- Mr. Zimmerman came up, the late ambassador Zimmerman, I think his name came up and I believe you have cited him on occasion and obviously I'm sure you're aware of his book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. He wrote a book called Origins of a Catastrophe: Yugoslavia and its Destroyers, America's Last Ambassador tells what happened and why. In his book, he describes some of the folks that he's met, does he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I don't have the book with me, unfortunately, in my rush to come here, but I do have the quotes, I'll give the page numbers and I can obviously provide the Court and the Prosecutor with the pages, copies of the pages but let me read you what Mr. Zimmerman says about these leaders. One gets sort of an impression of who Mr. Zimmerman is and what he thinks of the people he's dealing with. With respect to Milan Kucan, and you know who that individual is, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was he, for those of us who don't know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. He calls him squat and a human AK-47, whose lack of responsibility triggered the crisis in 1991. You will find that on pages 30 to 42 and on page 142. With respect to Alija Izetbegovic -- now, is that -- do you share that opinion of Mr. Kucan by the way, what you know of him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I probably don't know enough about him to form an opinion but I wouldn't start out at least by sharing that opinion of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I mean a human AK-47. That's rather rough, don't you think? That's like a machine-gun. Whose lack of responsibility triggered the crisis. I always thought the crisis was triggered because they were concerned about their vital national interests, considering that Milosevic there was rigging the game.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This characterisation, that he triggered the crisis. Is that your -- is that your opinion? Do you share that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. He characterises Alija Izetbegovic as "mild mannered to a fault, overly deferential and perpetually anxious and, like Franjo Tudjman and Vojislav Seselj, a nationalist who had been convicted of sowing ethnic hatred." That would be found on page 39 and 114 and to 115 of Mr. Zimmerman's book. Would you agree with that characterisation of Alija Izetbegovic, that he was convicted for sowing ethnic hatred? I take it that's when he was convicted during the former Yugoslavia days.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're reading from a document that I don't have in front of me and I don't know what the full context of it is. Your specific question as to the -- whether was convicted for sowing ethnic hatred, I would disagree, at least from a historian's standpoint. I'm not familiar with the specific charges that were filed in 1983 at his trial, but -- or for that matter in the 1947 trial. So I can't from a legal standpoint tell you that he was -- was or was not convicted of a charge of sowing ethnic hatred. I just don't have that information. But I would not share the characterisation of the purpose for which he was tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But when he was tried in 83, wasn't it because of a particular publication? Didn't he write something?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was that -- what was the title of it, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Islamic Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that Islamic declaration he expressed certain views which, I guess, the communist authorities at the time thought were sowing ethnic hatred?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't without reference to the specific charges answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you whether you've read that particular book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And that book, incidentally -- and there are various interpretations of the book, let me just stop with that question. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been a lot of interpretations of individual excerpts from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And varying interpretations of the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you know, some see it -- see Alija Izetbegovic as someone who aspires to protect and develop the vital national interests of the Muslim people in that region, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say one sees that in him, among other qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in that book, but in that book, others see him as a nationalist with a capital N?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that book, he never mentions Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So your assertion that he would in that book be advancing the national interests of the Bosnian Muslims is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, we are going to get into some disagreements here because that's not what I asked you. I'm saying others who have read this book have suggested, you know, from reading the book that he was a nationalist. I'm not saying that he was. I'm not stating an opinion one way or the other. But have others not, after reading that book, have suggested that he was a nationalist and some even have said that he was an Islamist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess my point being is it all depends on where you are from which spectrum -- from which school how you interpret this particular book. You may walk away with any one of those three or maybe even more opinions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can walk away from the book with just about any opinion you want to. Most people who opine on it haven't read it. They've read the excerpts which have become famous and widely cited but few people have really bothered to read the full text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which goes back to my part of the thing I talk about a little bit, my thesis is when you take something out of context, and you just read it and you fixate on it, then perhaps you might reach the wrong conclusion. I'm not saying -- I'm just saying in general now. So -- right? Is that a yes or no or maybe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree its your thesis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would agree if you take something out of context based on your answer to the previous question, folks have just read snippets of it, they walk away with all sorts of different opinions without having read the entire book. My apologies to the translators. Give them one minute to catch up.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. If your question was is it a bad idea to take something out of context, the answer is, yes, it is a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot help but let's say narrowing context in the course of selecting information but as much context as possible is always, I think, desirable --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in assessing these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, we won't go on any more with Mr. Zimmerman. He does talk about, describes Milosevic as a baby the baby-faced Milosevic, who was a master of media manipulation. I think we can all agree on that probably?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I failed to mention a couple of points that I wanted to drive home on this 27th December 1991 presidential transcript, so I apologise to everyone, especially to the honourable members of our Trial Bench but I need to go back and clarify a couple of points and this can be found on 61, page 61, of the -- of this particular document, which is P 00089. Page 61, you will see it says, Stjepan Kljujic, "Mr. President, with all due respect let me explain things a bit before leaving. I think I have the personal right to explain something to you. First, this is not a competition to see who is a greater Croat. If it were, I would not let anybody be -- we could only be equal. The idea of 13 June was mine. Mr. Vlasic developed it, Mr. Doko and I brought you the papers here, if you remember. Vice Vukojevic [phoen] and Mr. Ramjak [phoen] were present, as well. They were quite a few. Therefore I'm not against it but we agreed to put it into action at a certain moment. In my judgement it was not the right moment." Now, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, could we clarify something? You mentioned page 161. I have looked at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 61, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In an attempt to meet the time restrictions, I had to labour over night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we don't have this page in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. We can put it on the ELMO, Mr. President. We can put the particular page on the ELMO. I apologise. I assumed that the entire document had come in so we would have the full context of this presidential transcript. But we could place on the ELMO page 61. Perhaps Madam Usher could assist us with the -- or somebody. It's on the e-court. Okay. Again my apologies. All right. Now we see at the top of the -- rather, at the top of the page, Stjepan Kljujic and that's the section that I read where he talks about the idea of 13 June was mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, June 13 was a -- was a significant day in that that's when they set they had a meeting and they set the HDZ policy, joint policy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not looked at that document recently and.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's June 13, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my general understanding of what took place at that meeting. It was the first or maybe second meeting of the Croatian leadership subsequent to the meeting that Milosevic and Tudjman had at Karadjordjevo and therefore may have involved some discussion of the appropriate behaviour of the HDZ, BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the wake of that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it says here, Stjepan Kljujic is saying the idea of 13 June was mine. Mr. Vlasic developed it, Mr. Doko and I brought it, brought you the papers here. If you remember, and then he goes tonne and on. So it would appear, would it not, that the idea was Kljujic's?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he states here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in part, and again we have to read all 71 pages of this, but if your memory serves you right, would it not be fair to say that the principal discussion during this meeting with all these folks had to do with the Croatian question in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we flip to page 70 of this document, and if we could get it on the ELMO or on the e-court,. I apologise, I know that the folks in the Registry work very hard and Mr. Registrar is extremely efficient, as everyone else is. 70, page 70, could you put it on the ELMO? Maybe you could help us out here, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Maybe Madam Usher could help us out here. Page 70. We will get it right by the ends of this trial, Your Honour, I assure you that we are going to be working smoothly through this system. Okay. If we could look at this, and it's just a short -- it's -- this is towards the end, as I indicated, the document is only about 72 pages actually, to be correct. Here on page 70 they talk about setting up a commission. The president, we are talking about the late Franjo Tudjman, all right. Let's go. We said Kljujic, Boban, Vlado Santic, Iko Stanic, Udovicic, Lazic, and who else? Then you have Dario Kordic, that makes seven. And then he goes on again, Kljujic, Boban, Vlado Santic, Iko Stanic, Udovicic, Lazic, Kordic. Let's vote. So you see that, at least from here, that President Tudjman is setting up a commission, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is at the very end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And he's saying that these people must -- further down, he says at the end of the page, "These people must be in Sarajevo. You cannot have negotiations if people are coming and going. There may be intense negotiations lasting for two, three, four, or five days with the Muslims and then with the Serbs, if one person is from" -- and then it goes on. But basically, is it not at least if we look at this -- at the end of this meeting, as it would appear, since this is page 70 of a 72-page document, that the conclusion is that Tudjman is setting up a commission which includes, not excludes, Kljujic in order to negotiate with folks in Sarajevo, and by that it would be Izetbegovic and his team of advisers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the flow of the meeting is kind of important to understand. Tudjman convenes this meeting to hear the viewpoints of these various players and there is an extensive discussion in which people put forth their claims, their understanding, and Tudjman sort of hangs back, doesn't pronounce a decision on things, until he has heard all of these view points. And then I think about two-thirds of the way through the meeting, he decisively casts his opinion, which I think probably was known by many people there already, in favour of a territorial solution. The remaining problem is how to keep the party together, and I think this is really an effort to bring people back together. At least in one body, and bestow upon them the privilege of participating in the delegation, and I think Tudjman has -- you know, makes clear here that he wants to hear everybody out and earn their continued participation in the party even though Kljujic here is very transparently pleading for his job on the citation that you used earlier. He knows that the wind is not blowing in his direction, and so he goes back and reminds those present of the good things that he did, that is moving -- taking some initiative in the areas of protecting these -- at least having a discussion about the territories before he pleads for, you know, as he pleads for his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, well, party politics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean, might be -- we might soon be seeing that in England, you know, or the UK, with Tony Blair pleading for him to stay as Prime Minister with the backbenchers trying to get him to set a date so he can move along, right? It's party politics.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, but you know, when we read this and I'm sure we are going to did do this several times throughout the course of this trial, it would appear that what Tudjman is pushing for is a negotiated process, not a military one, but he wants the folks to sit down and try to find a negotiated solution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one important conclusion one can reach from reading this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the things I want to touch on, and again I know I'm going back and forth on various issues, and I apologise but I'm trying to live within the time limits, I want to touch on this -- on the European Community Conference that took place between 1991 and 1992. I think that you're aware of it. I'm going to show you a document. And this would be 1D 00417. And have you seen this document before, or a variation of it. It says, we can see at the top it's the editor's note?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at it, it says editor's note, "the efforts of the European Community Conference chaired by Lord Carrington," and then it has the treaty provisions for the convention of 4 November 1991. And it says here, at the end of the editor's note, "the text of the draft convention as of November 1991 is reproduced below."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you can just -- if you could look at the document a little bit, just to verify whether you've ever come across this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at just Article 1, we are not going to go through all of it but it says the new relations between the republics will be based on the following, and then there is a list, A, B, C, D, E, F. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, Lord Carrington, I believe his name came up yesterday, been around for -- was around for a long time, you know of him, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you know of meetings that he chaired in trying to find some sort of a solution for -- during the time when Yugoslavia was breaking up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to page -- it would be page 15, Madam Usher, numbered page 15. Item 3. It says there, let's rest our eyes a little bit, give everybody a chance to focus. It says -- it says there, number 3, "the republic shall guarantee to persons belonging to a national or ethnic group the following rights." And then I'll skip the first one, go to the second, "the right to be protected against any activity capable of threatening their existence." You see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All cultural rights. That would be number 2. We don't have to go through all of that, that bullet. Then the next one is protect -- "protection of equal participation in public affairs." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then at the bottom it says, "the right to decide to which national or ethnic group he or she wishes to belong." Pretty democratic, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't have much to do with democracy but it has to lot to do with human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Human rights, okay. I stand corrected. Human rights. I guess I kind of tie that one together but I guess as we are seeing in some places in the world, they don't co-exist sometimes. All right. If we flip the page and go to page 16, under the section of special status, again, let's rest our eyes a little bit. Give the folks time to catch their breath. Number 5 it says, "in addition, areas in which persons belonging to a national or ethnic group form a majority shall enjoy a special status of autonomy. Such a status will provide for, A, the right to have and show the national emblems of that area." B, is deleted. "C, an educational system which respects the values in each of that group." D, little i, "a legislative body." Next, "an administrative structure, including a regional police force, and third a judiciary responsible for matters concerning the area which affects the composition of the population of the area." And E, "provisions for appropriate international monitoring." Sir, in your research, have you ever come across, not this document, as you've indicated, any other documents that at least covered what was in the draft convention as we see it here today on this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a very broad question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of what was in this document before coming here today and me showing you a document which you had not seen, that is this treaty provision for the convention of 4 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would just observe it was -- it's dated as sort of the height of the war in Croatia, the JNA assault on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it may very well be intended to lay the foundation for the United Nations protection areas, the Serb areas within Croatia. I don't know that. I can't tell from the document and I don't have the context here to relate to it other than the fact that it provides these things, and I don't know also who may have drafted it, who accepted it, who opposed it, whether -- I'm quite confident it never became law and never became an international agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not suggesting that it did. It says draft convention. But if we were to take the editor to heart, the editor's note, okay, and we can provide the full volume of where all these documents are contained, it says, "the efforts of the European Community Conference chaired by Lord Carrington were focused on a draft convention containing articles dealing with," and it goes on. So let me ask you this: Did you ever study the documents generated from the negotiated efforts by the European Community and in particular Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't looked at the documents that pertain to the 1991 negotiations. I'm more familiar with some of the documentation from 1992, as the ECCY was moving toward the Bosnian independence and ultimately joined with the UN in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But it's fair to say, though, based on your knowledge of that period, that what is contained in this document, the sort of issues, the burning issues of the day within the former Yugoslavia as it was breaking apart, you know, the -- I'm speaking about human rights in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was designed to address those issues, yes, clearly, m'hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- all right. Do you know when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified yesterday, that was November 18, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And depending on this draft convention, it could have come either before or after the decision?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the draft convention is clearly 4 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's before the proclamation of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we would have had this particular document and then we would have the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. That will be enough for this issue. Thank you very much. Now, a couple of -- some other issues I need to just touch on a little bit. Probably going back to what we were just discussing, and that is the issue of nations, nationalities and what have you. And it would be fair to say that it's a rather complex issue, at least for some of us who come from places like the United States?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's complex for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And pretty difficult to think about having a nation or three nations within a territory or within a republic, whatever it may be. It's just the sounds of it, nation, is a little bit different, difficult to conceptualise except perhaps as Americans we are thinking of the Navaho nation, the Cherokee nation, at least that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I pointed out in the report, I think the word nation, which is literally translated people, is understood by most people in English to be an ethnic group or an ethno-national group or a nationality. All of which terms are unacceptable in their direct translation into B/C/S for native speakers but I think the point you make is well taken. The term nation as we view it in the Bosnia-Herzegovina context is -- requires a little bit of a conceptual leap to understand what they mean by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess when we are talking about nations and looking at Bosnia-Herzegovina because it had three nations, as Yugoslavia is breaking apart, that issue might become rather more important than it had been?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was true in every republic except Slovenia. There were communities in Macedonia, in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and certainly within Serbia which faced the same issue in one variant or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm not an expert in this area but I've tried at least to come to understand it or try to come to understand it, that the -- excuse me, that during the Yugoslav communist days, that was a rather significant issue and they made a distinction between nation and nationality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can -- if I understand it correctly, that nation referred to -- it's the homeland, but nationality is somebody else's homeland, they are living within somebody else's homeland?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of a nationality in, say, Yugoslav political thought, was that the major corpus of the people of that group lived in another polity outside Yugoslavia, so as I mentioned before the Hungarians of Vojvodina would look to Hungary as the homeland, if you will. The Albanians of Kosovo would -- the bulk of their corpus being in Albania but the concept guaranteed to these peoples something like equal rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- within the Yugoslav and republican political systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now there was also -- excuse me, there was also what was termed as a minority as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could just help us out, what did that entail?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throws were groups or members of groups that were -- didn't reach the status of either a nationality or a nation, would include, for example, Roma, Jews is a little bit problematical because they at one time had a different status but -- so there were Slovenes, for example, in Bosnia and Romanians, Germans, the whole complex of peoples with relatively small numbers who did not reach the status of either a nation or nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And when you said that the -- you said that the Jewish people had a different status at one point, picking up from that, it wasn't until sometime in the 70s that the Muslims had a different status within this question?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually go to the 1960s, but it was in the 1960s that the Bosnian Muslims achieved recognition as a nation on a par with Serbs, Croats, Macedonians, Slovenes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But whether was it codified in the constitution? I always thought it was 1974.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before that. There were constitutional amendments I think in 64 or 68 because it was in effect -- I believe that's correct. I would have to consult it to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, at the turn of the century, there was a national awakening, at least for the Muslims, where they began at some point to see themselves as a nation. I might have it wrong.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national awakenings really go back into the late 18th, early 19th century for the Serbs and Croats. I date the national awakening of the Bosnian Muslims to the 1960s, so much later than the other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it should also be clarified that they had their own political organisations, culture, all, let's say, the trappings of a nation as for back as the late 19th century, but did not, I would say, assert themselves through this national awakening process until roughly the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't pretend to know much about ethnography, as I understood it, when the Ottomans came to that region, a lot of folks converted into Islam.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so would it be fair to say that the Muslim people in that region, in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, are some, if not most, or all of the people that converted into Islam?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I missed your question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if those people converted and became Muslim, okay? Would it not stand to follow that the people that converted there must have been Serb or Croat before they converted, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their identity at that time was principally religious so in converting from, let's say, Catholicism to Islam which was the most common source of those conversions, they joined a new community. It's simply not possible to draw those sharp lines around a racial group which would say, these folks are Croats, and therefore their lineage for six, eight generations down are also Croats. That kind of, say, determination is simply impossible to make, and it appears that the primary source of identity for people in those times was religious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, with that particular issue, because if you look at -- if you go to the library you find a variety of opinions on, you know, who was where and who came from what period and there is a lot of controversy as far as, you know, who are the Croats, who are the Serbs, and who are the Muslims, at least in that particular -- in what is known commonly today as Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where they originated, how long they had been there, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that your interpretation is one of many that are held by historians such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the language, Serbo-Croatian, seems to reflect that at one point there were two languages. There was Serbian and Croatian, albeit they might have -- for all intents and purposes might have been the same language in a sense for some dialect differences but two distinct languages, right, Serbian and Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we -- I mentioned yesterday, the -- in the 19th century, there were efforts by both Croatian intellectual leaders and Serbian intellectual leaders in the first half of the 19th century to codify the language of the South Slavs, both of them interestingly based on dialects that were spoken in, principally, Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These codifications for the Croats were principally in service of the notion that the people who we were talking about were Illyrians, and then subsequently when they discovered that these really were not Illyrians but South Slavs they moved to a more Yugoslav orientation. The Serb codification of the language was -- kind of rejected this Yugoslav orientation at that time, so you had essentially two rival groups, if you will, of intellectuals trying to postulate different languages out of the same fundamental base of speech. So the -- there were many efforts over many years to bring these two languages into congruence, and the term "Serbo-Croatian" was convenient in the socialist period to -- communist period, if you will, to capture the fact that these languages were so close, but in the main, used different alphabets and used somewhat different but mutually intelligible terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But so if I -- if I may paraphrase you, make sure that I understand the concept, Tito comes along and fuses the two languages and calls it Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't -- I think it was a much more, let's say, extensive grassroots process than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't view it as a -- a Titoist diktat if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, I don't want to cast dispersions on, you know, Marsal, who's not here to defend himself. But nonetheless we had two different languages, now it's called Serbo-Croatian because, I assume, before that, the Serbs were speaking Serbian and the Croats were speaking Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on when you go out and take the pole and ask them what they are speaking. That sense of speaking that national language certainly strengthened particularly in let's say the first quarter of the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that at that particular time there was no Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would -- many people would contest that as well and point out that there was a Bosnian language that was specific to that -- the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In fact a grammar was published in 1908, I believe, and they cited the specific variant of the Cyrillic alphabet spoken in Bosnia which is called Bosancica, and cited documents going back many centuries that used this language. So certainly there was at least in the minds of many people a distinct language called Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's what was being taught at schools?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some time, yes, m'hm, in the Austro-Hungarian period essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right is that the same licensing that they brought back, now called Bosnian, because that was something that was negotiated at Dayton?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it wasn't negotiated at Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wasn't that part -- wasn't that injected into the constitution that there would be three languages --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- spoken in Bosnia-Herzegovina, known as Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian, not Bosniak, you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear, they are all south Slav languages and derived from essentially the same corpus of people and territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, just a moment, Mr. President. Well, I think that concludes my cross-examination at this point in time, to meet with Your Honour's time limitations. I would have liked to have more time and develop it more but in deference to my colleagues also that want to pose some questions. Thank you very much, Mr. Donia. Thank you, Your Honours. And I thank Mr. Scott for his patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, as to your documents, do you have a list of them? What do you plan to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Normally I like to go at the end so as not to take the time from my colleagues but since there are only three documents, I can do it right now. 1D 00398, 1D 00417. 1D 00416. These were marked for identification. If I'm wrong, I'm sure I will be corrected by Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you want them to be admitted or just marked for identification? We usually have them marked for identification when there is no translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess then they would have to be marked for identification until there is a translation. I'm still learning the process, Your Honour, but yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The following exhibits are therefore marked for identification, 1D 00398, 1D 00416, and 1D 00417. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will try to stay within the time limits. Mrs. Nozica asked me to leave perhaps five minutes for her at the end and perhaps even General Praljak will put a question or two, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Donia. My name is Tomislav Jonjic and I will be putting questions to you on behalf of Mr. Valentin Coric. Since we have only five or six minutes before the break, it seems that we will only be able to get to the introductory part. Initially I would like to check this. Can we agree that the writing of history is not just a mere chronology of events but that the task of historians is to establish not only the time when something happened but also the reasons for it happening, to show that human society, just like nature, does not make illogical leaps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the first part of your statement, that a major purpose of history is to do something more than simply create a chronology, but to explore the origins of reasons for something happening or not happening. Whether history makes illogical leaps or not is very much contested. I think there are so many things that happen against logic and you can even find people who would argue that logic is a very poor guide to follow in anticipating behaviour of human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't use this word logical, it was something inserted by the interpreters, and this prompted your reaction. Let us move to something else. Yesterday when answering Mr. Karnavas's questions, you agreed and said that it is possible, and rather that it frequently happens, that there are different interpretations of events, namely that historians very often differ when they interpret certain events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we know, based on your evidence yesterday, you mostly researched the Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1878 to 1918 or perhaps 1914. Does this mean that you do not consider yourself to be an expert for the entire history of Bosnia and Herzegovina or do you believe that you are an expert? It seems that the OTP believes you to be an expert for the entire history of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no longer the case that I have only done research on the Austro-Hungarian period. In preparation for my Sarajevo book, I've looked into all periods from the beginning of the Ottoman period up until, as I say, about 2000. I think one should let's say be cautious in the use of the word "expert" because if expert imply that is someone has examined every document and every source, I don't know that there is an expert on anything, but I have certainly spent time investigating, researching and writing upon every period of the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to some degree neighbouring lands, since the 15th century, not -- I really don't consider myself a medieval specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: If that is the case, then I will put some questions to you which are related to the previous period, the period prior to the events in the indictment. We will not go into early medieval history, but due to lack of time, we have less than an hour and a half for us, I would like to turn to details which are more relevant for my client and other accused in terms of the indictment. I try to be as brief and specific and I would like to ask you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I have prepared some ten to 15 books here, and about 100 excerpts but it seems that we won't be able to show any of these documents in view of the lack of time. However, we do have the books available here if we need to go into any details. You are don't need to worry. These are not samizdat or exotic books. These are elementary works and authors that you must be familiar with. You concluded that discussion with Mr. Karnavas by talking about the language, about the name and use of the language in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the former communist Yugoslavia. But you're not a linguist, you're not a language expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My approach to the language issue is one of a historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But despite of that, you said, yesterday on page 19 to 21 of the transcript, that the language spoken by Serbs, Croats, and Muslims is the same language called Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, and that the theses on the differences in the language is a very contentious one. That's what you said. And then you gave this explanation to Mr. Karnavas: "So I presume that we can move from there on. We don't need to wait for you to confirm my interpretation of your words." Therefore, I would like to ask you this: Do you know in what languages the Official Gazette of the SFRY was published, which was the official publication in which official regulations were published?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was published in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But however you don't know? You are just presuming this, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, it was published in Croatian, Macedonian, Serbian, Slovenian, not in Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. Yesterday we saw that without any difficulties, you are able to read the language you yourself call Serbo-Croatian and that you understand it in writing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear. I don't call it Serbo-Croatian today. One, I think, has to restrict the use of that term to characterise the language to prior to 1990. And I actually refer to it most conveniently as "the local language." But when I am reading a Cyrillic text by a Serb, I will refer to it as Serbian. When I'm reading a Croatian text by a Croat or a Latin text by a Croat, I'll refer to it as Croatian, and Bosnian. I try to make those distinctions, not always possible to make, but I'm not standing on insisting that the language today be called Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: If we have a couple of more minutes, I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have until 12.30. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, then. I misinterpreted the amount of time left to us. Could we then, please, ask the usher to put a document on the ELMO for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that to be done I will follow up on what you just now said, Dr. Donia. You said that up until 1990 there was a single language and that it was only recently that we saw that the language started splitting and that there were attempts to try to make the language be different. Now, we are going to see a sentence which I believe it to be quite a simple one and that everybody uttered this sentence in elementary school before 1990 or after 1990. And this is the sentence. Kitchen salt is a chemical compound of sodium and chlorine. The first line is in Croatian, the second line is the same sentence in Serbian, and then in the third line we see the same sentence in English. Serbian should have been written in Cyrillic but we didn't have Cyrillic font. Can we agree that all three sentences have the same meaning, that that neither of them has archaic words or any newly invented words, newly invented as a result of attempts to put in differences into the language after the 1990s' events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it seems that there are some certain differences between Serbian and Croatian and that they are not only lexical but also differences in syntax. However, we are not going to go into language debates here. I'm just interested in a detail that you as a historian must be aware of it. You must know that Bosnian Catholics and Bosnian Muslims, and I'm now referring to them as a religious group, speak Ikavian, they speak Ikavian dialect of Stokavian [phoen] language. Let me digress. For example, in the Bosnian church, the head was called Dik [phoen] and that this is an illustration of Ikavian that they spoke there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Bosnian church was the Dijed [phoen]. I would only -- I would agree but only say that the difference between the dialects is not purely a matter of national identity but also a matter of regional residence, or at least it was prior to say 1990 -- 1992. So you had neighbours in Mostar, for example, who spoke essentially the same dialect in the terms that you've just spelled out, who were from all three constituent nations and for that matter, could include members of minorities as well. So with the qualification that this was not strictly a national divide, I'd agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you there, absolutely. But let me first correct the translation. In line 25, on page 76 it should be Ikavian with an I, not Ekavian with an E. So I fully agree with you that the process of standardisation and mass media led to a situation where the language was somewhat standardised in urban situations but I'm interested in the language spoken by farmers, villagers in Bosnia, 30 or 40 years ago, and I would like you to confirm this, namely that Catholics and Muslims spoke Ikavian, and that orthodox residents whom we identify as Serbs nowadays, did not speak Ikavian.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't -- I mean, that's very difficult thing to know in my view because of the time frame you've put on it. But I think the gravitation of Bosnian Serbs to Ikavian actually was a function of wartime and you had a lot of Serbs who were speaking different variants of this, depending on residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then let us turn to a different topic. It seemed important for me to discuss the language issue because the common dialect spoken by Catholics and Muslims was one of the arguments invoked by Croatian integrational ideology in 18th and 19th century who believed them to be an integral portion of Croatian nation. This ideology was naturally a public one because it needed to be announced publicly, otherwise it would have had no purpose. This ideology was definitely formulated in the teachings of Dr. Ante Starcevic from the second part of the 19th century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it was an ideology that asserted that this was the common language of the Catholics and Muslims of Croat nationality, if you will. That was the argument. That was the ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that this ideology was popularised and spread from Zagreb and from Croatia, there were attempts to spread it into Bosnia as well. Without paying attention to the latest period, starting from the 1990s and on, prior to that, there was never any kind of an armed conflict between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia, isn't that right? I'm referring to the end of 19th century and the first and Second World Wars?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's a -- there were situations in which there may have been Croats on one side and Muslims on the other of a struggle, for example in the Partizan conflict during the Second World War, but if you state the proposition that, you know, vast majority of Croats were at war with the vast majority of Muslims, I would agree with your proposition, and in fact there was remarkably little armed conflict up until the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you. So the majority of Croats and the majority of Muslims in both world wars fought under the same flag and same coat of arms. Now that we've touched upon flags and coats of arms, let's look into this. You said yesterday on page 19 of the transcript something about use and abuse of national symbols, and in that context, you spoke about the spreading of Croatian national symbols in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't think we need to go into in depth heraldic discussions but we have definitely agree that the Croatian coat of arms is easily recognisable because it has in its central portion a chequerboard, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show us document 5D 01046? 5D 01046.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from a book. We have the translation into English. This is a book by Boza Mimica, Numismatics in the Historical Territory of Croatia, Fourth Century BC to 1918. Can we now see page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can see the following page, please? It's possible that we have it. These are page 457 and 460. Can we scroll down, stop there, please. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we have coins here of the king of Bosnia, Nikola Ilocki from the end of 15th century. You said that you started exploring the history of Bosnia from the 15th century onwards so you should know that this coincides with the time when the Turks came to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the fall of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not Bosnia in its modern borders but then borders. On this page, 413, we have a coin. Can we please see the next page? Once again, we have the coins of the same king. So these numismatic information about the material and the size of coins are not important to us but we can see that coins marked 414 to 422 have copies of the text where clearly you can see the word "Bosnia," and if I'm not mistaken we also see a clear symbol of a chequerboard which is to say the Croatian coat of arms. Then if we can go to the next page, please, which I think is the last page, that's right, yes. We see another one on the next page, let us zoom in. On the next page, the last coin is under number 422. There it is at the top of the page. Thank you. Dr. Donia, please tell me, am I right when I say that Croatian coat of arms can be seen in these coins?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the caption says. It says in the inner circle is the Hungarian-Croatian-Czech coat of arms for the -- number 422 any way. So it's Croatian in part, one presumes. And the same would be true of the other coins. I think it may be an error to conclude on the basis of this that this was a, let's say there was a huge Croatian nationally conscious population at that time. What I think this is, is a dynastic symbol of the time which at that time was indeed Hungarian, Croatian, and Czech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: No, Dr. Donia. Could we see the previous page, please? The previous one with coins 417 to 421? Dr. Donia, we are not now speaking of the population and the national awareness of that population. We are speaking of the coat of arms used by the hereditary ruler of the then Bosnia and it can be seen clearly on coins 417 to 421 that there is no mention of any Czech states or any other states, and that this is clearly referred to as a Croatian coat of arms. We are not speaking now of ethnic origin of the population living there but we are speaking of the symbol used by the hereditary ruler of Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I take the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now skip over several centuries, I have to ask you whether you're aware of existence of the Beg family Kopcic. This is one of the most prominent aristocratic Muslim families from the vicinity of Prozor. Have you ever come across that name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Despite of that, now that we are discussing coats of arms and symbols, I will show you one of the not numerous coats of arms that is included in Fojnica heraldic paper. Can we please see 5 D 01026. It's just an image without any text. All right. So this is the coat of arms of the Muslim family Kopcic from the 18th century, four years after the arrival of Osmani Turks to the area, included in the Fojnica heraldic paper. Can we agree, Dr. Donia that this coat of arms also has recognisable images?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the eagle is very, very widely used in just about every, in one variant or other in about he every family of heraldic symbols. The chequerboard shield is to be recognisable as a symbol of the Croatian king or Croatian state. Could also be a symbol of other things in that area or other areas. So I would want to see what the numismatic people think about what this stands for before I draw a conclusion on what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm actually asking you this, a Muslim family living near the border of the then Bosnia, and even today, that is only 20 to 30 kilometres as the crow flies from the territory of Croatia, so if such a family uses a chequerboard symbol, is it closer to Croatian coat of arms or is it perhaps closer to Mayas and Aztecs text?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mayas and Aztecs. The tribes and the people living in central America?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an absurd question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The answer is clear. Thank you. Since we have only two or three minutes remaining I'd like to conclude with this topic. Unfortunately we will not be able to show any of the other photographs I have prepared but perhaps you'll be able to confirm this without looking at the photographs. If we skip another two centuries now and come to the beginning of the 20th century. Yesterday you mentioned a meeting held at Siroki Brijeg which means you're familiar with that location, at least from stories you heard. You said yourself, you were in Sarajevo some times. Please tell me, did you see perhaps in Sarajevo, at the building of the Croatian cultural society called Napredak, which is one of the central Croatian national institutions, the building constructed early in the 20th century under the Austro-Hungarian rule. Did you see Croatian coat of arms on that building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you see perhaps a Croatian coat of arms on the windows of Croatian church which was constructed in Siroki Brijeg precisely at that period of time, if you ever visited the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the area about two weeks ago but I didn't get to Siroki Brijeg so in fact I've never been to Siroki Brijeg so I have not seen that particular structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When passing through Bosnia, did you see monuments erected to celebrate the 1.000 anniversary of Croatian statehood, that was in 1925 in many locations, such monuments were erected and invariably all of them have Croatian coat of arms. Have you ever seen them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a few of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The whole purpose of this discussion is to show that Croatian coat of arms in 1990 or 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina was nothing imported, nothing used there in order to illustrate national or state expansion, but rather that it was a normal symbol used by people who have lived there for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be an appropriate time to conclude before the break because after that I'd like to turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we will have a 20-minute break and we will resume at 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue with the cross-examination, of course, I'll give additional time to the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott wanted to take the floor to speak about the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. I know that time is precious but cannot end the week without talking about scheduling matters for next week and the following week. It may be easier, I think it will be easier, Your Honour, in case something might inadvertently be said about a protected witness if we could go into private session for the next couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this unless we go past 1.45. This is eating up into the Defence time. They went over an hour and a half yesterday. I think it's outrageous. It is eating into the Defence time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just before I give the floor to Mr. Scott, I said that the time Mr. Scott was going to take you would get it back. So we are going to count in minutes the time Mr. Scott is going to take and then it will be added to your time. Rest assured. Calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, regardless of the counsel conferring, I would like to proceed, in view of the fact that we have to finish at quarter past 2 today if I understand correctly and this means we have less than 45 minutes for the Defence of Mr. Coric. For this reason I wish to very briefly touch upon certain issues having to do with your expert report, and I wish to begin with the time period when you originally began dealing with Bosnia. In order to save time, I wish to read to you only two sentences from a book by Dr. Mustafa Imamovic whom you doubtless know of. He is one of the most eminent historians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He's a Bosniak and a Muslim, and in his book entitled, "the legal status and internal political development of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1878 to 1914" on page 98 he says the following: "In the time of the Kalaj regime in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for a long time the use of the Croatian name was banned. This was experienced by Stjepan Radic who travelled through Bosnia in 1891. Special attention was paid to prevent the party of rights ideology started by Starcevic from spreading to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Political links were banned, the import of newspapers from the triune kingdom," that refers to Croatia, "to Bosnia, was banned also." Would you agree with me that the Austro-Hungarian regime, especially during the time of governor Kalaj suppressed the Croatian name as well as Croatian propaganda in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as Dr. Imamovic says?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kalaj regime suppressed all national names, including the Croatian name, and forbade organisations with national names. I've actually quoted that extensively in my book on the 1878 to 1918, and it's a well-known, well-established fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. We agree, then, that the Kalaj regime attempted to create a Bosniak nation, a Bosniak entity, which would be multi-confessional or interconfessional, whatever the correct term may be.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: This attempt proved to be futile, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude from this that national identities had already been formed at the time among most of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Otherwise, there would have been no reason for such radical steps to remove the national identification of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not agree. I think you can say that the national identities were in the process of formation amongst elites in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. And it was due to the opposition of those elites that -- that that would be the principal reason that the project known as Bosnjasno [phoen] failed. I think if you -- and I think it's to look at the Austro-Hungarian approach to things, they were always dealing with elites. They were not engaged at all with the peasantry and even lower urban classes. So I would -- wouldn't say that the most of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina was nationally conscious at this time. A small stratum was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bosnian parliament in 1910 was organised on a confessional basis, not a national basis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both confessional and curial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, according to the information in the literature, how did the Muslim intelligentsia declare itself with regard to nationality, university Professors and students, civil servants and so on, not all, of course, but for the most part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two currents -- three. One which did not want to declare itself at all; one current of the -- you're talking about the Muslim intellectual elite that declared itself Croatian, and a third that declared itself Serb. In this time, I think the pendulum swung in favour of the Croatian identity because so many Muslim intellectuals studied outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, either in Zagreb or in Vienna and the regime prohibited anyone from studying in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I keep looking at the clock. Please tell us when talking about declaration of national identity, when the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was established in 1918, how did the Muslim representatives in the constituent assembly declare themselves, or after the first assembly elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substantial majority of them declared themselves Croats. Some, a few, declared themselves Yugoslav. A few declared themselves Serbs, a few declared themselves other, but I think something like 70, 80 per cent declared themselves Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and then in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, Svetozar Pribicevic I'm sure you're familiar with that name, you will agree with me that he was one of the key creators of the Yugoslav state, he was the first Minister of the Interior and a prominent politician, and I believe there is no doubt that you read his book, The Dictatorship of King Aleksandar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, perhaps, that Pribicevic, as a political player over three decades, and a very prominent player at that, says in the book that the vast majority of Bosnian Muslims felt themselves to be Croats with respect to nationality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT J. DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
